reference: U.S. Army Air Forces Type A-11 navigation (hack) watch, specification 94-27834, in its black-dial form of 1942 to 1945, made by Elgin, Bulova and Waltham. The caption names the A-11 and the drawing has its essentials: black dial, white Arabic numerals 1 to 12, minute strokes all round, white hands and a centre seconds hand, no date. The drawn smooth bezel is that of the 'waterproof' case and the plain stroke track matches the dial drawn in the wartime instruction handbook; the other issued case, the 'dustproof' one, has a coin-edge bezel, and one Bulova dial I saw adds a railroad ring. Three drawn features are not A-11 at all: the inner 13 to 24 ring, the darts at the hours and the syringe hands come from later U.S. issue watches (to my knowledge the A-17 and the GG-W-113 family; not checked on a page I read in full). Finish decision: the A-11's bright chromium-plated case is kept, not the dull grey case of those later watches, because the caption fixes the model and the decade; the borrowed markings are treated as more flat white print, which is how every A-11 marking is done.

surfaces.material: chromium-plated brass (occasionally silver or stainless steel)
surfaces.detail: Bright plate: Worn & Wound says the cases were 'generally chromium-plated brass'. No text I read states the factory polish in words; it is read from photographs. An unissued Elgin still on its factory tag is mirror-bright all over, and the worn Bulova that Worn & Wound shows is still bright on the bezel. The drawn bezel is the smooth type of the 'waterproof' case, which a collector tutorial describes as having 'a two stepped appearance': a low outer ring and a narrower inner one round the crystal. The unissued Elgin has the other, coin-edge bezel, so the bright finish on the smooth bezel rests on the worn Bulova alone. On worn watches the plate thins and warmer brass shows at the high points.

surfaces.material: chromium-plated brass (occasionally silver or stainless steel)
surfaces.detail: The case middle shows from the front as a narrow rounded shoulder outside the bezel, in the same bright plate with no brushing and no chamfer (mirror-bright on the unissued Elgin).

surfaces.material: chromium-plated brass (occasionally silver or stainless steel)
surfaces.detail: Thin, slightly curved lugs carrying the same bright plate, with no brushing and no chamfer; drilled for spring bars and 16 mm apart (Worn & Wound). Mirror-bright on the unissued Elgin.

surfaces.direction: knurling parallel to the stem (9 to 3)
surfaces.detail: Plain unsigned crown, 'notched for easy grip' (Worn & Wound), with coarse straight knurling and fairly large for the case. Bright on the unissued Elgin; dulled to grey on the worn Bulova.

Plain black dial with no maker's name (the tutorial: 'No maker on dial'). Black is stated in every source; the low sheen is read from photographs and is satin-matte, not dead flat, on the unissued Elgin.

Arabic numerals 1 to 12 and the minute strokes are flat white print; the real dial also carries small numerals 10 to 60 outside the track (the tutorial: '60 second tic numerals only on the 10s'). The drawn 13 to 24 ring and hour darts are not A-11 features and should be the same flat white print, never applied or raised.

The standard Air Forces A-11 is not luminous (the tutorial: 'Not lumed'; Worn & Wound notes that unlumed and lumed versions were both produced, the fully lumed one for the Navy). Markings and hands are therefore plain paint with no raised or glowing compound.

Flat hands painted white and dark at the hub (the tutorial: 'White but black at the base and not lumed. They are tapered'; a dealer's summary of the type: 'Black dial; white hands'). The real shape is a tapered lance; the drawn syringe outline comes from later U.S. issue watches but takes the same flat white paint.
Thin white centre seconds hand of constant width with a short tail, as on the unissued Elgin, the Bulova that Worn & Wound shows and the wartime handbook drawing.

Small pale metal hub at the centre of the hands, bright in the photographs of the Bulova and the Elgin. Its finish is not described anywhere I read, so polished is only a reading from those photographs.
Domed acrylic standing well above the bezel: Worn & Wound says the crystals were specified as unbreakable acrylic and the tutorial that they 'were domed and plexi'. Originals have yellowed with age.

surfaces.part: bracelet or strap at the lugs
surfaces.detail: One- or two-piece canvas strap in olive drab, as laid down in the War Department handbook (Worn & Wound). The unissued Elgin is on a one-piece khaki-olive cotton strap that passes behind the case, so plain woven fabric shows between both pairs of lugs.

surfaces.part: other (parts this watch does not have)
surfaces.detail: No bezel insert or markings, no rotating bezel, no crown guards, no pushers, no date, no sub-dial, nothing applied to the dial, no maker's name, no screws visible from the front, no brushing and no chamfers.

lightBehaviour: The chrome bezel, shoulder and lugs are the brightest parts: on so small and rounded a case the lamp shows as a tight hot highlight that runs round the bezel as the lamp moves, against dark reflections elsewhere, in a slightly colder white than steel.
The dial does nothing: flat black and flat white paint, with no sparkle and no raised edges to catch light.
The white hands are matte; a low lamp throws their thin shadow onto the dial but they never flash.
The domed acrylic carries a broad soft reflection of the lamp and a bright ring where the dome meets the bezel, and it softens the edge of the minute track.
The knurled crown gives a row of small glints; on a worn example the bezel highlight breaks up and warm brass shows at the edges.
geometry: Small round case about 32 mm across with a narrow smooth bezel in two low steps, a rounded shoulder of the case middle outside it, and thin slightly curved lugs 16 mm apart, about 39 mm from tip to tip. One knurled crown at 3 with no crown guards; no pushers, no date, no rotating bezel or insert. Nothing is applied to the dial and no screws show from the front. High-domed acrylic crystal. Olive drab canvas strap on spring bars between drilled lugs.
avoid: The dull grey case of the later U.S. issue watches and of modern A-11-style field watches: the 1940s case is bright chrome plate.
Brushing or polished chamfers on the case; the plate simply follows the pressed shape.
A coin-edge bezel: it exists on the 'dustproof' A-11 case but is not what is drawn.
Raised or glowing lume on the numerals, darts or hands; the standard A-11 is flat white paint.
Polished steel or gilt hands; they are painted white.
Reading the 13 to 24 ring, the hour darts or the syringe hands as a reason to use a later watch's finishing; they are borrowed layout only.
A maker's name or a date on the dial, a sapphire crystal or crown guards.
